itions

Incorporation

This is the creation of a new legal entity. The Companies Act 2006 covers the incorporations of companies and the Limited Liability Partnerships Act 2000 covers incorporating LLPs. Learn more about incorporation.

Restoration

A restoration is the process by which a dissolved entity recorded on a Companies House register is returned to that register. Restoration may apply to companies and other registrable corporate bodies, such as LLPs, where the relevant legislative requirements are met. An entity that is restored is generally treated in law as having continued in existence as if it had not been struck off or dissolved.

Depending on the type of entity and the circumstances of its dissolution, restoration may be achieved either through an administrative application to the Registrar or by an order of the court.

Strike off

Strike off is the removal of a company from the Companies House register. This generally occurs not less than 2 months after the first Gazette has been issued to a company, if no other action has happened between this time. Learn more about closing a company.

Dissolution

Dissolution is the legal outcome once the strike off process is complete. At that point, the company ceases to exist as a legal entity. This generally happens within one week of the company being struck off.

Because of these timeframes, a company that is struck off in one month may not be dissolved until the next month.

Other additions and removals

The register size can change when corporate bodies convert to another corporate body. For example, when an LLP becomes a limited company.

Removals from the register

A company can be removed from the register through several routes:

liquidation

voluntary strike off, where the company chooses to be removed

compulsory strike off, where the Registrar takes action to remove the company - this usually happens when there is reason to believe the company is no longer trading or operating, or it has failed to update its registered office address from a defaulted address

expedited strike off, where there is reason to believe the company was formed on a false basis

First Gazette notice for strike off

Companies undergoing voluntary, compulsory or expedited compulsory strike off will be issued a first Gazette notice for strike off. Following this notice, the company will be struck off and dissolved in:

not less than 2 months for voluntary strike off, unless the strike off application is withdrawn

not less than 2 months for compulsory strike off, unless the registrar is provided sufficient evidence to the contrary

not less than 28 days for expedited compulsory strike off, unless the registrar is provided sufficient evidence to the contrary

Companies may take longer than the minimum stated duration to be struck off and dissolved, for example if there is an objection to the company being removed from the register.

Learn more about objections.

Final Gazette notice for strike off

Companies are dissolved on the date that a final Gazette notice is issued. The final Gazette notice can be for a company that has:

dissolved following voluntary strike off

dissolved following compulsory strike off, this includes companies dissolved by expedited strike off

dissolved following liquidation

dissolved following a court order

Jurisdiction

This is the name of the official power to make legal decisions and judgements. This responsibility lies with the Registrar. There are roles within Companies House for a Registrar of England and Wales, a Registrar of Scotland and a Registrar of Northern Ireland.

passages.quote:
1. Overview

This guide provides quality and methods information for our ‘incorporated companies in the UK’ publication.

We publish statistics on UK companies register movements every quarter, with a monthly breakdown of each measure. These include additions to the register, such as incorporations and restorations, and removals, such as strike-offs.

These statistics come from administrative data held on the UK companies register. The data is collected mainly to run Companies House’s operations, such as processing company filings and applications. We carry out quality assurance and sense checks before publication. This helps us identify and address issues that can arise from using operational data for statistical purposes.

These are statistics in development. For more information, see the section How we quality assure the data and statistics.

2. Latest changes to quality and methods

We updated this guide on 30 July 2026. Important changes to quality and methods since we previously published this guide on 31 October 2024 are:

publishing a monthly breakdown of information - published quarterly

improving our tracking of company movements, so that additions and removals now add up to the change in register size

no longer publishing the effective register and the number of companies in the course of dissolution as a headline figure, and instead publishing detailed breakdowns of company status

providing a more detail on the stages a company goes through when it is removed from the register

For more information on latest, past and upcoming changes, go to the section Changes and their effects on comparability over time.

3. What the statistics cover

We publish a quarterly release, with a monthly breakdown of the following register movements:

total register size

additions to the register, including incorporations, restorations and other additions including conversions to a company

removals from the register, including first Gazette notices, companies being struck off and dissolutions

a breakdown of removals by whether a company chose to be removed voluntarily or followed a compulsory route

The publication covers two types of corporate body: companies and limited liability partnerships (LLPs).

The UK companies register covers England and Wales, Scotland and Northern Ireland. We publish monthly figures for companies and LLPs, both for the UK as a whole and for each of these areas.

3.1 What the statistics do not cover

These statistics cover companies and LLPs registered with Companies House. They do not include:

unincorporated businesses, such as sole traders and ordinary partnerships, which are not required to register with Companies House

the total number of businesses in the UK, since these statistics count corporate bodies registered with Companies House rather than businesses more broadly

For statistics that cover the wider UK business population, see the section Comparability and coherence with other statistics producers.

4. Where the data comes from

These statistics come from administrative data held on the UK companies register. This data is collected mainly to run Companies House’s operations, such as processing company filings and applications, rather than to produce statistics. We use this same data to count activity on the register, such as incorporations, removals and changes in register size.

Companies and LLPs must tell Companies House about certain changes, such as incorporations, changes of directors, and applications to be struck off. This information is submitted through our online, paper and API filing services, and is recorded on the register at the point it is processed.

All the figures in this publication come from this single source.

5. How we produce the statistics

We extract data from the companies register on a monthly basis, using the same records Companies House uses to run its operations. We do not independently verify the accuracy of information filed by companies.

We use agreed definitions to classify each transaction, such as incorporations, restorations, strike offs and dissolutions. This code is written by our analysts and checked by others with the right expertise.

We check that additions and removals add up to the change in register size for each month, and investigate any figures that look unexpected before publishing.

We combine the monthly figures into quarterly totals. The quarterly total is always the sum of the 3 months, with no separate adjustment.

6. Quality of the statistics

6.1 Statistical designation

These statistics are labelled as ‘official statistics in development’. They are based on information from our main operational database, accessed via a cloud-based data platform. We are developing how we collect the data and produce the statistics to improve their quality.

Once we have completed the developments, we will review the statistics with the Statistics Head of Profession.

If the statistics meet trustworthiness, quality and value standards based on user feedback, we will remove the official statistics in development label to publish under the ‘official statistics’ label.

If they do not meet trustworthiness, quality and value standards, we will further develop them and might stop producing them.

We will inform users of the outcome of our, and any Office for Statistics Regulation (OSR), review and any changes.

6.2 How we quality assure the data and statistics

Quality assurance is completed at a number of points during the publication round. This section will go into the different forms of quality assurance performed at each stage.

Quality assurance at the point of data extraction

We ensure that the correct records, transactions and events are captured. The actions taken during this period are:

independent reviews conducted on extraction code to validate the logic, filters and transformations

liaising with subject matter experts and colleagues to discuss the approach to writing code
